Black Mesa is a fantastic remake of the original Half Life. it is a must play for any Half Life fan and a great entry point for new comers. It took me almost 17 hours to finish this game.

I like how this not a 1:1 remake of the original. Crowbar Collective have done a fantastic job of adding their own flavor into the game in terms of puzzles and map design. I dreaded a few maps from the original because of how confusing it was. I was expecting the same here but I was happy to report that those maps were redesigned to not be so confusing.

Movement is not as fluid or fast as the original(Its the same as Half Life 2 if you have played it) but I have no complaints on this front and no complaints with the platforming sections. 

The gunplay is very familiar if you have played Half life 2. The weapons are the same as the original(models have the same design as the original but look better) but with quality of life changes for the guns. The animation when you first get a weapon is a very nice touch(Especially for that one weapon you get later on in the game, you'll know it when you see it).

The guns especially the shotgun sound very impactful. When I first listened to the first few music, I was like its' alright but it keeps getting better as you play the game. That one section of the game had in my opinion the best music in the game([spoiler]Battle music that plays in the Gonarch's Lair[/spoiler])

Coming to the map design, as mentioned Crowbar Collective have added their own flavor in terms of puzzles and map design. They have incorporated similar puzzle design as that of Half Life 2 and its expansions which provides a nice break from the combat. They weren't difficult to solve but it does take a few minutes to figure out the solution.

The enemies are same as the original except with a few additional varieties in Xen. Don't have much to say about them other than they were fun to fight.

Coming to Xen, it is very beautiful compared to the original. [spoiler]This section got a complete overhaul. I can see why this section took a long time to finish. It is almost completely unrecognizable. They did keep small sections similar to the original but the rest is completely different.  And I mean different in a good way. They added set pieces that show the science team have been to the borderworld for some time(this was barely shown in the original). I also like how the Vortigaunts are friendly until a controller takes control over them. The Vortiguants even help you sometimes. This added lore really shows why the Vortiguants revere Gordon so much in Half Life 2 and is a fantastic addition to this game[/spoiler]

The voice acting is good. It is difficult to notice the differences from the original voice actor of G-man and the voice actor who plays as him in this game.

This game has some replay value if you want to do the challenges listed in the achievements but other than that it is a linear story driven FPS so not much reason to play again if not for the aforementioned achievements.

Note: I haven't played the multiplayer.

In conclusion, this is a really good game and as mentioned a must play for any Half Life fan. 10/10

This is a mod I've followed since the early days. I remember checking their website every month or so hoping to see a new render or screenshot. When that first trailer dropped over 12 years ago, I was blown away. This was the version of Half-Life I had to play. The animation on that blast pit tentacle was superb. It looked better than any other fan game anyone had seen. 2009 it said.
2009 came and went. Radio silence befell the Black Mesa Source devs and for years, the ETA became a blanket "when it's done." The Source engine was rapidly losing its new car scent. Were the devs losing interest? Were they lying low in fear of Valve's lawyers? Was there any hope for this mod?
The game released in 2015 as a "Greenlight" title, which was an initiative allowing Steam users to vote on which games would be added to the Steam store next; a process which thankfully became much easier later on. Not only did this confirm they had Valve's blessing, it enabled them to monetize a project they had volunteered countless hours to. 
I admire Crowbar Collective for sticking with it. I can't imagine how hard it is to coordinate a volunteer project this size with no expectation of getting paid for it. I also admire Valve's sensible attitude toward modding their games. Cooperating with your fan community is mutually beneficial and seems like a no brainer. I don't see why other companies like Nintendo are so quick to send a cease and desist when a fan project gains traction; It only breeds contempt in those most passionate about your brand. 
Black Mesa is still actively being developed as of 2020 and is nearing its Definitive Edition release. The game didn't blow me away like I'm sure it would have in 2008. The novelty of ragdolls and DirectX 9 lighting has worn off. I'd still recommend playing Half-Life first, but Black Mesa is a beautiful remake. Especially the Xen areas. With enough Steam Workshop magic you can make it sound and feel more like the original. My criticisms are honestly pretty minimal. I think Black Mesa deserves recognition among the other great Source engine games.

[h1]Quick Summary[/h1]
Black Mesa is not just your typical 'updated graphics remake' ordeal. This is a front-to-back [b]rebuild[/b] of the original Half-Life game. I'm a long time Half-Life fan, and playing this felt like an entirely new experience. Not only are the graphics and audio massively improved from the first game, but the gameplay is far more engaging. I'm still trying to process that this [b]wasn't[/b] developed by Valve. Whether you're a new Half-Life fan or a veteran, you absolutely need to play this game. If the original game's age is a turn-off, I would say that Black Mesa is a fantastic way to introduce yourself to the universe. It's all here.

[h1]My Full Review[/h1]
There's so much that I could talk about regarding how fantastic this game turned out. The recreation of Xen is absolutely a highlight, but I feel like it goes without saying that Black Mesa is a far better game overall than the first Half-Life. There's a lot to see and a lot to interact with. Seeing varied NPCs, hearing new voice lines, and seeing familiar places with a refreshed and modern look is only the tip of the iceberg.

The gameplay is well refined. I'd go as far as saying that Black Mesa feels better to play than Half-Life 2. The Crowbar Collective took everything Valve did with Half-Life and developed more fully realized puzzles, fighting encounters, environments, and platforming. The stunning visuals and use of lighting work wonders in creating a living, breathing world of chaos and isolation.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
Black Mesa just feels different in many ways. Every weapon just feels really good to use. Damage values feel consistent, and the gunplay is overall pretty satisfying. Every encounter in the game provides encouragement to use your whole arsenal in varied ways.

The enemies are actually pretty difficult! Marines lob grenades frequently and feel relentless with their gunfire. Zombies vary slightly, but overall they feel about the same as you'd expect in any Half-Life game. All of the Xen enemies, however, are far more challenging and feel quite a bit more disruptive than I remember them being.

There's a lot to say about the Xen gameplay. The platforming feels [b]very good[/b] compared to the original game. The recreation of the various levels in Xen provide all-new puzzles and encounters that really match Valve's way of thinking. Everything in Xen fits right into what I'd expect from a Half-Life game and then some. I was worried that Xen was going to be a shot-for-shot recreation, because it's definitely not my favorite part of the original game. Thankfully, this isn't the case, and the love for this game's success absolutely shows. The biggest issue I have with this game shows up in the Interloper chapter, as it feels like it drags on a little too long.

[h1]Story / Plot[/h1]
Considering this is a remake of the original Half-Life, the story is still just as fantastic. What's great about Black Mesa is that the team piece together some of the retcons Valve made in Half-Life 2. The game feels like it fits in the Half-Life universe better than the original game for this reason alone. Talking to the various NPCs will reveal some little details that nod to things mentioned in Half-Life 2. I definitely prefer and appreciate this direction, because Half-Life always felt so detached from Half-Life 2.

The additional details with the recreation of Xen also align much better with the events in Half-Life 2. Vortigaunts attack only because they're enslaved. When you reach them in Xen, it's clear that they're a passive bunch until mind-controlled. This passive display is also shown in Half-Life 2.


[h1]Graphics / Audio[/h1]
The visuals are absolutely stunning. Lighting is used very effectively, and you'll be using your flashlight more often than you'd think. You'll find yourself running down steel corridors covered in bloodstains, broken glass, and bio-hazards. Cold steel tiles and walls contrast strongly with the rusted frames and rocky exteriors. Black Mesa makes it [b]very[/b] clear that you're traversing through a scientific catastrophe.

The visuals used for Xen are just on another level. I never thought i'd see such a beautiful environment in a Source game, yet here we are. The vibrant blues and purples strike a fantastic otherworldly ambiance never seen in a Half-Life game. Dense star fields and and gaseous elements fill your surroundings as you hop from rock to rock. The vivid forests feel familiar yet uncanny, and the ominous oranges and reds bleed a sense of brooding evil.

The audio received a fantastic overhaul as well. Weapons are quite satisfying to fire, and all of the effects feel full-bodied and harmful. The clicks, snaps, and impacts feel like what a refreshed source game should sound like. The new voice lines and voice actors also fit right in. I was pretty skeptic about how they would pull off some of this, but nothing felt out of place. If anything, I was surprised with how far the voice acting goes.

And last but not least... the soundtrack. It's [b]too good.[/b] Every track that played accented the various environments and circumstances perfectly. If you don't play this game, just go listen to the soundtrack, because it really stands out on its own.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
Black Mesa is a brand new experience rebuilt from the popular Half-Life game. Every moment of this game was genuinely intriguing and felt quite loyal to the original game wherever necessary. This feels less like a mod, and truly more like a full game. If you already love Half-Life, I doubt you'd be disappointed.

This review will be divided into two parts, because it frankly needs to be. 

You see, there are really two components to Black Mesa.  The first component is the obvious one - the remake of Half Life 1 as a Source Engine game.  In this regard, Black Mesa succeeds quite well.  The Black Mesa Research Facility is brought to life in a way GoldSrc could have never managed, and even though I know the entire game like the back of my hand, I still had moments of surprise and engagement that kept me pushing through; Half Life 1 is, even today, still a very fun FPS experience, but Black Mesa takes what was already a great game and builds on it.  With the benefits of modern-ish technology, Black Mesa is the definitive way to experience the original game that started it all and kickstarted an era of FPS gaming.  It's clear that the development team had a very serious respect and love of the source material, and the few significant changes they do make to the game's structure enhance it rather than detracting from it.  

Having gotten that out of the way, let me move on to the second part of the review - Xen. 

The original Xen was, for a time, the poster child for disappointing final levels in gaming.  I can't say that I ever felt this way myself, but many people found it to be an under-developed idea that didn't take advantage of the idea behind it.  Having played Black Mesa's rendition of Xen through, I finally understand why people felt that GoldSrc Xen was a disappointment.  There are few games on the market today that can truly capture a sense of genuine wonder and beauty; Subnautica remains the premier example in my mind, and Black Mesa's Xen has now joined those illustrious ranks. 

BM takes the original idea of Xen and successfully elevates it beyond what the original developers could have ever imagined; breathtaking visuals and an excellent soundtrack will keep even the most hardened Half Life veterans invested in the experience, living up to the potential lying behind a strange and unspoiled border world in the far reaches of space and time.  

I mentioned before that the development team had a clear love for the source material, and Xen is the culmination of that love; although this section of the game is expanded so dramatically that it quite easily adds several hours of gameplay to the experience, it's all done in a cohesive and consistent manner, one that takes into account the established lore of the Half Life universe.  Rather than feeling like a noticeable expansion through adaptation, it feels like a missing piece of the puzzle that should have been there to begin with.

I would go so far as to say that having played Black Mesa would be PREFERABLE from a ludonarrative standpoint; among other things, it adds serious context to the Vortigaunts' loyalty to Freeman from HL2 onwards.  This is all capped off with a final throwdown with the Nihilanth that makes the original boss fight look like a comedic parody in comparison.

In summary, if you intend to play Half Life 1, Black Mesa is a realization of virtually all of the potential the game had, brought up to (relatively) modern standards.  HL1 was a landmark title, but BM does everything it did better, and then some.

This is a remake done right, it respects the source material and improves upon it greatly.

It's impossible to overstate how much of a game changer the original Half Life was at the time. The opening 15 minutes consisted of a monorail ride through the expansive Black Mesa research facility and small talk with the coworkers. By this point, before anything of any significance had happened, I was all in. FPS games had been around for nearly 10 years, but none had introduced storytelling beyond 'shoot the bad guys' and maaaaybe 'find the blue key.' But Half Life introduced an actual plot and story line: at a top secret research facility in New Mexico, an experiment goes awry and opens a rift with another world and you, playing scientist Gordon Freeman, are one of the few survivors. You need to try to escape the facility while avoiding a government containment and clean up team.

But alas, Half Life got old and it *felt* old. The story was still stellar, but the graphics were stuck in the late 1990s. That's where Black Mesa was born. Black Mesa isn't really a reboot or a remake, it is more like a digitally remastered Blu-ray release of an old movie: sharper picture, better audio, maybe some deleted scenes, but by and large the same story nearly scene-for-scene.

The graphics in Black Mesa aren't GREAT, but they're certainly several steps above the original and they're enough to make the game feel modern enough. I got those same tingles on that opening monorail ride and had a wide smile on my face when re-encountering familiar chapters I'd played 21 years before. And the 'Zen' maps, depicting an other worldly planet that Freeman encounters later in the game are oftentimes downright gorgeous!

That said, Zen is also the only knock on the game for me. I'll admit, I wasn't a big fan of the Zen chapters in the original Half Life. I liked the familiarity of the earth-bound Black Mesa research facility and jumping to another astral plane with different gravity, toxins and creatures just felt like too much of a hard turn for me. I emphasize the 'FOR ME' there, as I realize it's subjective. While the Zen levels in Black Mesa are truly beautiful, it feels like they're also significantly longer than they were in the original game. I'm going off of memory here but it felt like Half Life, the research facility chapters made up about 70% of total time spent in the game while Zen chapters made up the remaining 30%, while in Black Mesa I spent about 10 hours each in the research facility and the Zen chapters. For someone not all that keen on Zen to begin with, more Zen did not make Black Mesa a better experience. Finishing the 'Interloper' chapter in the Black Mesa remake was more of a laborious chore than an exciting adventure. It was a very lovely laborious chore though.

All in all, Black Mesa is a nice way to enjoy the original 1998 Half Life experience through the eyes of a 2012-ish computer engine, and if you've not played the original Half Life then Black Mesa is definitely a game worth acquiring.

A game like Black Mesa is one of the riskiest a developer can make. You're taking a beloved piece of gaming history and remaking it. The original Half Life was a gaming juggernaut, so what's the risk? Ask the producers of the Ghostbusters reboot. When you start messing with peoples' great memories, you run the risk of really getting yourself in hot water.

Well, make no mistake: Black Mesa is *exactly* the game those brilliant developers at Valve had in mind when they made the original Half Life. Don't get me wrong; I'm not denigrating the original, not by any stretch of the imagination. I own two copies -- the original CD and my new Steam copy -- and I'm going to continue enjoying the original. But Black Mesa really is what that game wanted to be. It just has the advantage of having software that wasn't even a twinkle in an engineer's eye back in 1998, and consumers with rigs that can make the most of that output. If Valve were making Half Life today, I'm sure Black Mesa is what it would look like.

But make no mistake, folks: this is NOT a direct remake. You, like I, may know the Half Life levels forward and backward, where every goody is, and where every weapon is. Well, forget it. In giving HL its facelife, the Black Mesa developers moved, tweaked, and subtly altered the game. You'll recognize rooms, places, and sequences with nostalgia. But that shotgun in the security cage with the guard? It ain't there. You won't be able to take your old Half Life knowledge and speedrun Black Mesa. And, in my estimation, that's a good thing.

There are new environmental puzzles. The facility, even in its run-down sectors, is gorgeous eye-candy all the way. Little unobrusive easter eggs (like the Black Mesa emergency procedures signs) add flavor to the levels and give we old-timers a nod without breaking the world immersion. That Crowbar Collective has dedicated thousands of person-hours to this project is obvious: this masterpiece is a labor of love.

If you're a Half Life fan, a Portal fan, or just like a good atmospheric shooter, this is a must-buy. I'll admit it freely: I was leery of this title. "How do you remake a game like Half Life?" I kept asking myself. The answer? Like this. This is how it's done.

[h1]INTRODUCTION:[/h1]
Black Mesa is a first-person shooter game by the 'Black Mesa Modification Team' aka 'Crowbar Collective' serving as a total HD remake using the Source engine of Valve's critically acclaimed and award winning game Half-Life (1998). Although Black Mesa originally started out as a simple Half-Life 2 mod, it has since developed and evolved into its own standalone game.

Black Mesa still follows the original Half-Life 1 story (albeit with a few level redesigns) where the player takes on the role of Gordon Freeman, a scientist working for the Black Mesa Research Complex with a PhD in Theoretical Physics with an uncanny ability to wield human and alien military hardware. Follow him as he fights his way through the Black Mesa complex which is under siege from Alien invaders following an experiment gone horribly wrong and the military who's out to cover-up the incident.

[h1]PROS:[/h1]
+ Immense Graphical Improvement from the original game, such as, but not limited to:
[list]
[*] High Resolution textures
[*] Improved particle effects
[*] Improved lighting effects
[*] Good gun models and textures
[*] Good animation quality
[*] Good character models
[/list]
+ Improved immersion and atmosphere that brings the Black Mesa Complex to life such as, but not limited to:
[list]
[*] New NPC to Player dialogues and new NPC to NPC conversations
[*] Diverse NPC models including female scientist, guards and soldiers with varying uniforms and faces
[*] Great sound effects
[*] Revamped voices of Marines and Aliens (Vortigaunt)
[/list]
+ Great voice acting
+ The AI for Black Mesa Security Guards were significantly improved (they now have a better chance of survival than the Barney Calhoun clones from the original game.)..but... (See CON #6)
+ Cool soundtrack that plays on specific levels and events
+ The level redesigns opened several new small areas within the levels and chapters which encourages a bit of exploration
+ Customization options for multiplayer characters
+ Good game time (provided you're playing for immersion rather than a speed run)
+ [url=http://www.blackmesasource.com/]Free version (Legacy Version) of Black Mesa is still available for download[/url]
+ Great over-all presentation
+ Steam Workshop Support

[h1]CONS:[/h1]
- Early Access (will remove after final release)
- Half-Life 'Xen' chapters are still missing (will remove when its completed)
- Longer than usual load times
- Walk button is not functioning properly
- Few minor graphical glitches (particularly, some blood stain on the hand and guns models don't disappear)
- The Marines and Scientist AI needs improvement (The Scientist Escort AI runs into line of fire instead of taking cover; In some occasions the enemy AI just stand around like turrets.)
- Some of the redesigned levels feels a bit shorter than the original versions. (To be more specific, 'Surface Tension' and 'On A Rail' chapters.

[h1]CONCLUSION:[/h1]
[b]GREAT GAME[/b] that does the legendary Half-Life franchise justice and Lord Gaben proud. Brought to us by a team of volunteer artists, coders and developers, Black Mesa proves that the formula of Half-Life can and will withstand the test of time. 

Both fans of the old title and the next generation of gamers can once again visit the universe that revolutionized FPS gaming. 

[h1]WORTH IT?:[/h1]
I can easily [b]RECOMMEND this game even at its full price[/b] of $19.99 (or your regional equivalent). Black Mesa provides at least 8-10 hours of game time with one playthrough and is highly satisfying to finish.

Sadly, my childhood self couldn’t grasp the basic tutorial and ended up getting stuck in the actual tram when I was supposed to get out.

At 13, I nearly finished the game, but the Xen part frustrated the hell out of me. The difficulty ramped up, and without much games experience, I eventually abandoned it.

Fast forward 12 years, and here I am. The graphics of the original game haven't aged well, and with this remake already available, I opted out with this. While it doesn’t have a fully modern look (essentially using Half-Life 2 assets), the graphical improvements become evident as you progress through the levels.

Black Mesa started as a mod and evolved into a standalone game that was updated for five years. Some parts of the original game, particularly the Xen portion, were initially missing but were added back for the full release in 2020.

I enjoyed most of the game, much like I did with the original, but what really stood out to me was the reimagined Xen part. They essentially recreated the Black Mesa levels 1:1 but went bonkers with Xen. Although it doesn't carry the same eerie atmosphere as the original, the rework is much more impressive.

The Xen levels have been entirely overhauled to align more closely with the rest of the game. Unlike the original, which was dark and open, this version is more linear and refined. They cranked up the intensity for the last part, making it feel much more modern compared to the earlier sections. It features kickass boss fights and fun puzzles.

The hype and excitement I felt before and after the final boss fight is what ultimately made me really love this remake.

Addendum:

[b]XEN[/b]

Perhaps the only subpar section of the original game, underwhelming after what was an outstanding Adventure, it felt like Valve rushed through Xen.

The same clever puzzles were there, interaction and combat wise, it was a worthy ending to the title.

Visually however, Xen was a disappointment in half life.

NOT ANYMORE.

After I passed through the Lambda portal, I knew I was in for a treat, hell, the visuals from the portal itself are jaw-dropping...  and perhaps i was misremembering, but the level itself is MASSIVE, alternating between puzzles, combat, platforming and running for your life.

Crowbar Collective has improved on every aspect of Black Mesa's Final chapter.

The entirety of the realm feels alien, yet believable.  Weird and wonderful, everywhere you look you are greeted with pure visual spectacle, surreal, deadly eye candy.

The Flora and Fauna are believable, with the exception of the entirely gravity defying nature of the landscape, but I suppose that's part of Xen's phantasmagoric allure.  Despite this, it still comes across as a believable biome, the various monsters that had tormented you on your journey through the Black Mesa complex are shown in reasonable context, intrinsic parts of the environment, both in locomotive capability, and camouflage.  The creatures appearances and offensive capabilities are explained, without a single word, by their unnatural habit.

The environmental puzzles that allowed Gordon Freeman to Weave his way through the Black Mesa complex also exist in Xen, I have to commend the developers on the fact that none of it felt obvious, the pathways you would need to take to get where you were going are intrinsic parts of the environment, they look like they belong there, not that they merely exist to facilitate Gordon's Passage.

The sound design is fantastic, blending the odd noises of the creatures with further environmental sounds, creating the impression of an alien rainforest, brimming with life, and very much seeking to take yours.

Xen's natural properties explain why Black Mesa was so interested in researching the place, both for it's levitating materials, as well as elements of a natural origin which were capable of generating tremendous electrical (and otherwise) energy.

I recommend moving cautiously through the area, visually identifying Environmental hazards, and how to use them on your enemies. Even on medium difficulty, ammo is scarce.

There are a few surprises, and I'm going to leave it at that.

Like every other part of the game, the completion of a puzzle leaves you with a tremendous feeling of satisfaction....  it's an added bonus, that the entire time you are more than happy to stop and take in the scenery.

No one has done first person puzzle-platforming better.
The Gonarch is the Gold standard for boss fights. 
Nihilanth is also fantastic.

When I finished this game around 4 years ago I thought that would be it. Apparently the devs were working on 'Xen' levels at the time but the game was in development for 10 years at that point already so I wasn't going to hold my breath for it. But that was fine as it was such a pleasure to play through anyway, even if Xen is never finished and no improvements are made, it was definitely worth my time and whatever amount of money I paid.

I then saw at the top of my library some news for this game, that Xen was actually finished. When I booted it up my saves were no longer compatible but thankfully the game still remembered I had finished the previous chapters and let me skip to Xen.

It almost immediately took my breath away and I found myself exploring every corner once again. It has the same feel as the Half Life games, puzzle-heavy, fast, science fiction character-driven shooter with no cutscenes. You're always excited and dreaded to see what's around the corner or behind the door.

Now what makes me especially happy is that these levels, albeit promised in the past, were added at no extra cost. I bought the game on sale and about 4 years later I get extra fun content and improvements to it for free. In exchange for that, I'll leave a positive review.

Is relatively rare for me to write a thoughtful review, in Eng especially, but some things just have to be done.

I've played Black Mesa a few years ago, back in in the days when it was a mod, before Xen. And still it surprised me a lot.

Original Half Life was a game that, to a certain extent, revolutionize a FPS genre. Among many other things, it introduced the way how story could be embedded seamlessly into game world, without countless cutting, without even leaving main character "head". Also, usage of "show, don't tell" formula, although it's all about simple mechanics and engine from 1998, is still remarkable today. What's actually funny is that even today there are still many games that deeply dependent of TELLING you things. Like, a lot of games. Ones that treat player like a over-protective mother treat her only child, telling you exactly what to do, barraging you with on-screen hints, or telling you some background story you have no real emotional connection with. Even games that universally recognized as "good" do that, sometimes. Ahem... 

So, the first half of Black Mesa is, basically, carefull recreation of first Half Life, done with greatest love to original material and with modern technologies of Source engine. It so true to original that, if you played HL1 a lot, you would certainly will face situations like "Oh, I remember that place, there should be a vent down there!". Only minor changes were made, mostly utiliazing modern(ish) physics of Source engine in few "physics puzzles", or slightly reducing the "impact" of more boring parts of the original game (like railroad section, in Black Mesa it feels less boring, slightly shorter and more eventful). You don't have to put bricks on planck to build a bridge, but if you played HL2 and Episodes - you already know what kind of "puzzles" I'm talking about. Enemy AI is also, obviously, updated. Alien creatures bite hard, but in the first half of the game it's mostly Marines that will really make you suffer. And in certain conditions - suffer a lot. Their clever usage of terrain, group tactics, suppresive fire and grenades force you to seek for any advantage possible. You have to be fast, agile, smart and able of adapting to a constantly evolving situation to survive. I bet on easier difficulties it feels less so, but I've played it on maximum difficulty only, and even with full HP and Energy under direct fire from squad of Marines you'll live someting around 3 seconds.   

And then there is Xen...

Original HL creators, like Marc Laidlaw, stated few times that Xen was a "last minute addition", and at first they wanted Xen to be different, but engine limitations and time restrictions couldn't allow that. Even if you in deep love with HL1, you would probably knew it already. Original Xen feels like a real definition of a word "lackluster" - there was nothing special about it, and "boss battles" are wery pale. But hey! Here is some platforming, go jump around...    

Black Mesa's iteration of Xen is, indeed, everything Xen could and should be. It's not just recreation now, it's expansion. Visuals, artstyle, sound design and OST, level design and overall "narrative" structure is really out of this world (pun intended). From the first seconds it shows to you, lound and clear, that it's not game about aliens from other dimension invading Black Mesa Research Facility - now it is game about Xen and [i]YOU are alien[/i] here. Addition of few enemy types are most welcome and seems entirely logical, like they are already belonged to Half Life universe. [strike]Why the hell there wasn't any HEV Suit-wearing zombies in the original game in the first place?[/strike] And then there is fight against Gonarch, which makes original looks like a bad joke. It constantly evolving. One moment you are hiding from it in the caves, next - you are firing rockets at it from a distance, and next thing you know - you are running from it, with little to no ammo, through a crystal-forest, praying to Schrödinger's Cat that turn you make previously in a hurry would lead to supply drop or pre-planted explosives - and not to pit into endless void. 

Last parts of Xen are better left without spoilers, but it revolving around Gluon Gun in (roughly) the same manner as HL2 ending revolving around Gravity Gun. And it's so freakin' intense that sometimes it makes TOHOU Project games looks like pre-sleep ASMR videos in comparison.

If you are not indifferent to HL universe, or just wanted to expirience what classical FPS could be - buy it. With no hesitation. Totally worth it's money.

Just make sure your computer can handle the game's dynamic lighting.


Black Mesa started as a free mod, but with the effort put into its development over eight-plus years it might as well be a whole new game - all because they were dissatisfied with Valve porting it to their then-new Source physics engine in 2004. Pretty much every aspect has been remastered, and Workshop support lets you modify your experience easier than ever before if you so wish.

With the release of the Xen levels in 2020 marking the official launch of Black Mesa 1.0, this remake was in development for [i]sixteen years[/i]. The fact that it's out now shows true dedication and passion, and the finished product well deserves a pricetag. Black Mesa Xen itself is a definite improvement over Half-Life Xen, bordering on a complete redo of that whole section of the game; although it does drag in parts, it's still pretty solid. You could even say the more content the merrier, if you already loved the game.

If you're not familiar with Half-Life, well, you don't have to be to jump right in. A Valve employee who worked on the original Half-Life [url=https://www.pcgamer.com/half-life-alyxs-level-designer-would-rather-play-black-mesa-than-the-original-half-life/]outright stated they preferred playing Black Mesa instead of the original game[/url], citing the sheer quality of Black Mesa's execution (not that the original game isn't playable if you're more retro-inclined, of course - it's just 22 years older.) If you're looking for a solid FPS that doubles as a solid [i]experience[/i], with some brains, tension bordering on survival horror at times, and maybe even a little pathos up its sleeve, you should definitely consider Black Mesa.

And hey, there's multiplayer included with good maps and decent netcode. It's quite similar to HL's deathmatch if it were at the speed of HL2 Deathmatch, with a much wider range of player model choices. The actual gameplay is still old-school 'player who gets the best guns first gets to kill everyone quicker' for better or worse, and there's usually not many players, but it's there.


These are more technical details/notes for people who've played the mod's original release or the original Half-Life:

Black Mesa's dynamic lighting can be pretty taxing on your system if it's not powerful enough. For the 1.0 release I had to turn a lot of the settings down, especially said lighting, and play on a lower resolution. The game still looked pretty good and it was well worth being able to play it, of course.

Maps have been streamlined from the mod's first launch and from HL. The gameplay itself is different from HL in only one way: it's generally better. The HECU Marines no longer quite resemble hideously overpowered aimbots.

The only criticism that could be said of the campaign is that the devs made it noticeably harder than the original HL. At times, this makes the game somewhat frustrating unless you know what to expect for some areas. Although considering you're effectively playing Dr. Joe Schmoe and fighting highly trained US Marines, it might be thematically fitting. And to be fair, game players have also had two decades to get better at playing games.


BM's graphics, as you might know, could be described as an improvement. Every security guard no longer looks the same. There's actually women scientists now. The Marines have much better voice acting. The 'Black Mesa' tab in the options menu lets you configure a lot of the game's new graphical effects, such as sideways movement bob, revolver ironsights and houndeye tinnitus. The music is also pretty good. Not quite as iconic as the original music, but it definitely shines at times.

BM's most beautiful improvement to me, though, is the weaponry. The arsenal's feel is massively improved over the original Black Mesa mod's guns, and every one of them is good in their own right. I'd say they give the original game's weapons a good run for their money in terms of satisfying use.


Given all of this, Black Mesa is well worth paying for, both as a treat for Half-Life fans and as a great action game for new players. Even if you didn't like the original Half-Life for whatever reason, I would still recommend trying it.

[h1] From Black Mesa with love [/h1]
In many ways Half-Life was a revolutionary game when it has first seen the daylight in 1998. Imagine fully functional companions who followed your command. A groundbreaking technology that gave characters facial expressions. An FPS that had an actual story and one told via gameplay on top of that. All of those were impressive to say the least, over 20 years ago. That said, it is an obviously aged title, especially in terms of graphics. Back in 1998 Valve in many ways was venturing into uncharted territory. Certain standards we are used to in video games haven’t been invented yet, let alone established and popularised. Alas, despite being a trend-setter Half-Life also inevitably had its flaws. Flaws that Crowbar Collective decided to replace with fun, and updated graphics. Truth be told, not only the developers were mostly successful in delivering this premise, Black Mesa goes way beyond [i]just[/i] fixing mistakes, making for a proper remake.

[b] The same but different [/b]
On the most basic level Black Mesa is Half-Life remade with graphics fit for 2020. Truth be told, many players won’t delve any further than this and it’s perfectly fine. The devil truly is in the details of Black Mesa. Only if you have played the original Half-Life before, will you be able to truly appreciate the scope of changes introduced. While being Half-Life at heart, Black Mesa takes the liberty of retelling the story in its own way, rather than strictly adhering to the source material. For starters, the game’s story has been altered as to represent tying the two Half-Life game’s together. Instead of countless clones of scientist_model_2, you get to see familiar, albeit younger, dr Kleiner or Eli Vance. Vortigaunts now too have a role to play, much bigger than just being another alien assailant. Questionable ethics chapter is much more fitting to its namesake, featuring some quite shady contraptions, and the list goes on. Crowbar Collective time and again displays a deep understanding of Half-Life’s strengths and weaknesses and the entire game had been adjusted accordingly.

My biggest complaint of confusing level design,[url=https://steamcommunity.com/profiles/76561198010155821/recommended/70/] that I had with the original game [/url] is simply gone. Tedious sections (I am looking at you, railcart) has been shortened and refreshed with more action or new puzzles. Awkward area transitions had been streamlined and remade as to be organic and intuitive. Furthermore, the interactive elements necessary for progress are now nicely lit-up or uniform as to remove any confusion. Finally, the exploration feels rewarding and universally allows a quick return to the “main route”, rather than have you backtrack aimlessly as the original did. Long story short, I haven’t been lost once in Black Mesa and it was a blissful sensation. 

By far the greatest departure from the original happens in Xen. Rather than being a strict finale of the game, the venture into borderworld is greatly expanded in Black Mesa. Now divided into three distinct chapters, Xen is a fully-fledged final act of the game lasting, for roughly 5 hours. The scenery is no longer strange and angular, Xen of Black Mesa is foremost mesmerising. Creative freedom was utilised to the maximum when the alien planet was created mostly from scratch. Now it is filled with diverse and beautiful sceneries with multiple vantage points just screaming „screenshot” at the player. 
[url] https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2082309675 [/url]
[b] Unforseen consequences [/b]
Being the most creative part of the game, I do consider Xen to be the definite highlight of Black Mesa as a whole. On the second hand, for the very same reason the final act of the game can also be the most divisive. The multiple chase sequences that force the player to fully utilise the new jumping module may very well be a turn down for many. Gonarch boss fight also has been recreated into an entire chapter of the game. You are first introduced to this unstoppable force of nature that not even the rock walls are able to stop, to then have a final showdown after multiple earlier skirmishes. Frankly the fight has been improved to such an extent that it outperforms the final boss in both build-up and difficulty. Especially given that the factory leading to the big bad of the game is the only part of Black Mesa that I found tedious. I can acknowledge that the tedium is partly drawn from the source material, still, it drags on to the point of almost delivering you half-asleep for the final confrontation. One conveyor belt at a time. 

Then there is the matter of physics. They are beyond a shadow of doubt better than in Half-Life. Unfortunately, when compared to how leaps and bounds ahead everything else is, the object physics do seem like a weakpoint of the game: items party sinking in the concrete floor, a guard literally exploding because their toe got stuck under a pallet, getting instantly killed after the turret I carried collided with thin air and crushed me to death. They were ultimately few and far between, though if you experience any shenanigans during the play, physics are likely to be at fault. Fully aware of that, the developers even smuggled a little bit of fun into that mix - when exposed to overwhelming damage, the enemies erupt into a shower of gore and gibs. The shotgun feels more powerful than ever before.

[b] Cascade of fun [/b]
Probably the most interesting aspect of Black Mesa is that the game is a fan-made project. Instead of being simply canned as many such endeavours, Crowbar Collective’s love for the game was allowed to flourish, resulting in a truly quality product. This title was created with an idea of giving Half-Life an overall upgrade, as to make it fit for a contemporary player. With the ground premise soundly delivered, the developers carried on, giving Black Mesa enough new content and changes for the game to have a hint of its own identity. If you are among the players who played HL 2 first, and are not exactly fond of oldschool anymore, the origin story is now ripe for the taking as Black Mesa. Should you happen to be a fan of the franchise, the game instead becomes a love-letter that just keeps on giving, the more you delve into the details. If Half-Life franchise holds any water to you, Black Mesa is a must-buy title. On the off-chance you never heard of the franchise before and simply enjoy the FPS genre the game is also highly recommendable. It has a 15-odd hours long campaign filled with diverse environments, distinct cast of enemies and unique choice of weapons. Shooters like these are not really made anymore and you get to experience a piece of gaming history along the way. The proverbial HEV armour may have few dents but it shines nonetheless. Feel the weight of trusty crowbar in your hand and onto the fray you go. In Soviet Russia the aliens are invaded by you.

The modern reimagination of the timeless masterpiece. It takes the original immersive complex of Black Mesa and expands it immensively. It also displays some of the story and lore more clearly, and more importantly it stablishes the bridge absent between Half Life 1 and Half Life 2. Can't go wrong playing this instead of HL1.

This is an excellent fan-made remake of the original Half-Life game. I thoroughly enjoyed the first part where Freeman has to escape the facility; It kept true to the original story and maps while also adding some additional rooms and spaces to explore. The introduction, just after the Resonance Cascade event, is even more atmospheric and spookier than the original - adding in the half-zombies was a great touch. The soundtrack is also marvellous; Internal Conflict by Joel Nielsen goes too hard.

However, this game is not without its flaws. It did crash on me a couple of times, but most often during the Nihilinth boss fight. Unfortunately, I did spend a good chunk of time relaunching my game and reloading uncorrupted saves before the crash trying to figure out how to defeat the boss. It took me far too long to realise that the rocket launcher was doing negative damage to its brain (makes sense) so once I swapped to the tau cannon I easily overcome it and was able to finish the game. Getting thrown out of bounds may have also added salt to the wound...

The Xen level is absolutely gorgeous (so beautiful in fact there are entire guides on how to farm it for screenshots). Visually extremely stunning and rich in fauna and flora I actually preferred this over the original. The alien levels do drop off a bit in quality as they go on. The Interloper chapter was particularly tedious and repetitive, some parts poorly construed and thrown together. Perhaps the developers were also running out of steam towards the end.

This game is well-worth a play-through but is by no means a replacement to the original which I believe remains the GOAT.

It's a modernisation of a classic gaming legend in the best way, staying as faithful to the original as possible, while improving it in almost every conceivable manner. Crowbar Collective have taken exceptional care in the detailing and crafting of a far more believable and liveable world than the original, especially so in the Lambda facility and offices, and the truly spectacular and phenomenally imaginative overhaul of Xen, a sequence of levels that I once thought bland, frustrating and forgettable now one of if not my favourite locale in Black Mesa. It's gorgeous, and incredibly engaging.

There are still constant jarring issues I've come across with regards to stability, particularly during said spectacular Xen sequences, where it would often hang and require force closing, or hard crashing to the desktop without any error dialogues, once making it impossible to proceed without hanging, which was solved by just loading a prior save slot. I've also experienced cases of the graphics driver crashing and reloading. I'm not seeing a lot of similar mentions in other reviews, so this may just be due to my system age/configuration, so grain of salt and what not.

Other than the technical hassles, this is a triumph in remastering and the passion of fan works, and I hope this team of gigachads get to outdo themselves again in the future.

I would argue this is the de facto best way to experience Half Life 1 in all its glory. The original is an indelible piece of gaming history, but Black Mesa has brought the experience up to par with its timeless influence.
Laughably easy recommendation to anyone considering it a purchase.

What to say? The first half of the game is updated, improved version of the old classic that we know and love. Until we get to Xen. The first time Gordon teleports in, it is absolutely gorgeous. Xen is now half of the game, and is worth the asking price on it's own - it is completely re-designed, re-scored and refreshed. I found myself spending a good few minutes standing there, looking up at the environment each time after emerging from a cave system, with the score swelling around me taking in everything. It really is excellent. Joel Nielsen has done a superb job on the soundtrack - it is very hard to believe that this is a fan made game in every aspect - and is a credit to everyone who worked on it for so long.

There are a few niggles - getting stuck on scenery occasionally, some of the sections felt a little bit too long and in one later battle with the Alien Controllers my 970 struggled with all the particles, dropping to 10fps (at 1440p) but a game restart cured that after finishing the section. I'm nitpicking, however. Don't let it put you off, the experience is worth it. Completed in February 2020.

Everything leads up to the Nihilanth fight, an exposition which is tremendous. A climactic battle in it's truest sense, with the amount of destruction that rains upon you as it gets closer to the end being truly awe inspiring. No hyperbole. I was very impressed.

Crowbar Collective should be very satisfied with themselves. Well done all of you!

Black Mesa is a remake of Half-Life that has been around in one form or another for many years, but its road to completion nearly turned into a shitstorm thanks to the seemingly endless development of the Xen chapters.

Even calling it a "remake" feels as though it doesn't quite do the game justice. Since the developers themselves use that term, though, we can safely go with it. Personally, I think of Black Mesa more as a reimagining.

Black Mesa was first released in 2012 as a free mod and later arrived on Steam in 2015. At that point, however, the final sections of the game, commonly referred to as the Xen chapters, were still missing. For years, the game effectively ended at Lambda Core, just as Gordon Freeman was about to leave the Black Mesa Research Facility and teleport into the alien world of Xen.

That finally changed in March 2020, when the Xen chapters were completed and version 1.0 was released. I only managed to finish these new chapters some time later, with the pandemic finally giving me enough time to sit down and experience the completed game properly.

As for the sections that had already existed since 2015, Black Mesa did an excellent job of capturing the spirit of the original Half-Life while carrying it forward.

It is, after all, a reimagining of a game from an era when games rarely took players by the hand and politely guided them toward the next objective. Because of that, some chapters can feel considerably more difficult than what modern players may be accustomed to.

But the environments are carefully constructed from beginning to end, the atmosphere is wonderfully oppressive, and the way Half-Life begins as an almost painfully ordinary workday before gradually descending into complete chaos has been recreated beautifully.

For anyone unfamiliar with the story, here is a brief summary. The original game is old enough now that plenty of people reading this were not even born when it was released.

The Black Mesa Research Facility is a massive, high-tech underground research complex located in New Mexico. You play as Gordon Freeman, a 27-year-old scientist who is already running late for a particularly unusual experiment.

After the famous tram ride, changing into your iconic HEV, or Hazardous Environment, Suit, and greeting your colleagues, you eventually enter the enormous test chamber containing the Anti-Mass Spectrometer.

This is where every ordinary part of Gordon's day ends. The moment the experiment begins, portals start opening to an unknown world and unidentified creatures begin pouring into the facility. This event, known as a "resonance cascade," leaves Black Mesa devastated. You wake up as one of the survivors and begin trying to escape the enormous complex.

Eventually you learn that the military has arrived. Unfortunately, your brief hope of rescue disappears when you realize that they are not exactly there to save anyone. Their mission is to silence every surviving member of the facility's personnel, including you.

At that point, all hell properly breaks loose.

I also want to talk about the Xen chapters without going too deeply into spoilers.
In the original Half-Life, Xen was easily my least favorite part of the game. I have completed the original numerous times, and those were always the chapters I was least interested in replaying.

Black Mesa, however, transformed Xen into something else entirely.

The newly added chapters are enormous, to the point that their combined length feels almost comparable to much of the Earthbound portion of the game that had already existed since 2015. The scale of the new maps is difficult to overstate.

Some players will undoubtedly become tired of the repetitive puzzles after a while, but Half-Life has always been as much a puzzle game as an action game. As someone who still remembers how irritating some of the original Xen puzzles could be, I found Black Mesa's approach considerably more enjoyable and intuitive.

Graphically, what Crowbar Collective managed to achieve with the Source engine is extraordinary.

Black Mesa did not always look this good. Over the years, the developers continuously improved the lighting, environments, effects and overall visual presentation. The sections inside the research facility still hold up remarkably well, but Xen is where the game becomes genuinely breathtaking.

And yes, breathtaking. Although obviously not as breathtaking as Keanu Reeves.

I lost count of how many times I simply stopped moving during the first Xen chapter and stared across its enormous alien landscapes, suspended islands, strange colors and endless void.

From completely redesigned enemies to heavily altered level layouts, Black Mesa does more than simply pay tribute to its predecessor. It stands on the shoulders of the already legendary Half-Life and, in many places, actually manages to raise the bar.

The newly composed soundtrack is another major success. It retains the spirit of the original while establishing an identity of its own, and thankfully it is readily available on platforms such as YouTube and Spotify.

Mild spoilers from this point onward.

I want to talk specifically about Gonarch and Nihilanth, the major bosses of the Xen chapters.
The Gonarch battle is considerably longer than it was in the original game, and some players have complained about this. Personally, I loved it.

Some of the chase sequences are admittedly a little forced, and the fact that Gonarch is invulnerable during certain moments is not communicated particularly well. Players can easily waste ammunition firing at something they cannot actually damage.

Still, playing hide-and-seek with this gigantic, single-balled monstrosity creates a genuine feeling of struggle and desperation that was almost completely absent from the original encounter.

Nihilanth is an even greater improvement.

He feels vastly more majestic and threatening than he did in the original Half-Life, which is exactly how he should feel. He is the final boss, after all.

The entire encounter gives you the unmistakable sense that you have finally reached the end of a very long journey.

Most importantly, the developers removed his incredibly frustrating ability to teleport the player out of the arena. Instead, Nihilanth now has several different abilities that appear throughout multiple phases of the fight. As his health decreases, the encounter becomes progressively more intense.

This finally turns Nihilanth into the climactic final boss that Half-Life deserved in the first place.

Then there is Interloper. This chapter has been criticized to hell and back, and I understand why. I got tired of it in several places as well.  But something many people seem to forget is that Interloper was always like this in the original game.

So yes, that elevator is literally carrying you toward the final boss, and the game throws almost everything it has at you while you're going up to make sure you feel it. Admittedly, that sequence may be several leagues outside the comfort zone of players accustomed to having every solution delivered on a silver platter. But that is partly the point. You are playing an old legend, rebuilt to modern standards without completely sanding away the teeth that made the original memorable.

In the end, Black Mesa has probably introduced thousands of players to Half-Life who either could not experience it when it was originally released or would never have considered playing it today because of how dated the original graphics have become.

Crowbar Collective did not merely modernize Half-Life.

They took one of gaming's great classics, treated it with enormous respect, rebuilt its weakest sections, expanded its world, and somehow managed to create something that can stand proudly beside the original.

For the amount of work that went into accomplishing that, they deserve both a salute and an applause.

What is Black Mesa?

Black Mesa is a remake of Half-Life which was released in 1998. In 2004, two teams known as Leakfree and Half-Life: Source Overhaul Project both wanted to create remakes using the new Source Engine. Instead of being rivals, they joined forces and became Crowbar Collective (CC). And created the Black Mesa that we know today. The main reason why they wanted to remake Half-Life was to experiment with the tools on the Source Engine. 

This project as been going for just over eight years and it has attracted the attention of not just gamers, but many talented programmers and developers to join CC and improve on the game. It has also inspired developers to remake the Expansion Packs from Half-Life such as: Blue Shift, Opposing Force and Decay (and that CC are approving and are also being made on the Source Engine)

Despite its success, I have noticed some negative reviews:

Many people are annoyed and are refunding the game since it's Xen chapters haven't been released yet. It was set to be released in the Summer 2017, then it was delayed since CC wanted to improve it and subsequently set for release in December 2017. It was recently delayed again to a date which we are still waiting for the developers to announce. Bear in mind that this is an EARLY ACCESS GAME, the developers upload what they have already done and gradually add and improve as time goes by. The game is getting closer and closer towards its release and we (as a community) have helped them fix bugs and small details in the game.

Should I buy this game?

If you have played the original Half-Life in 1998, then you will definitely enjoy this game. Maps and levels have been recreated and expanded and graphics have been improved to make it as realistic as possible. However, if you don't know anything about Half-Life but are interested, I recommend that you wait for it to go on sale instead of buying it at full price.

Black Mesa is the gold standard for remaking an older game. Most remakes tend to be ports to newer consoles with higher frames per second or slightly-better graphics, but Black Mesa goes above and beyond the minimal effort that companies put into their re-releases. It shows that, sometimes, a fan project can surpass AAA games of the same genre.

If you've played Half-Life, you already know the story of Black Mesa. An experiment gone awry results in an alien invasion at a New Mexico research facility, leaving you to escape the disaster area and figure out how to set things right. Not much has changed in terms of pacing, but some improvements over Half-Life's level design have been implemented. Annoying sections like On a Rail's maze or We've Got Hostiles' vent tunnels have been heavily cut down. The mod has a better overall "flow" to it than Half-Life, though a couple levels like Apprehension still drag on.

The graphics are stunning. Crowbar Collective has pushed the Source Engine to its limits, and it shows. Everything in the facility feels vibrant and real. The game has pretty good optimization as well, meaning that lower-tier computers should be able to play it smoothly with reduced settings.

Black Mesa's gameplay feels fluid. Quality of life changes, like sprinting and infinite flashlight battery life, make navigating the levels less of a chore and more of an adventure. All of the classic weapons return looking sharp and mostly unchanged. Enemies from the original game are less sluggish and far more deadly than before. Don't underestimate anything, as even the simple Headcrab Zombie poses a far greater threat than you'd think. 

The Steam version of the game has some features that the 2012 mod lacks. There is a multiplayer mode and support for Steam Workshop. Weapons look and animate better. Most of all, the HECU Grunts no longer have their cheesy Solid Snake voices like they did in the mod! Now they sound like soldiers caught up in an unpredictable conflict, not canned voices from an action movie.

Joel Nielsen did a great job with the game's soundtrack. I would recommend checking out his website after you've beaten the game. My personal favorites from the album are "Questionable Ethics 1" and "Forget about Freeman."

All in all, Black Mesa is a solid first-person shooter that harkens back to the old days of save scumming and exploration. I would recommend buying it if you're a fan of the Half-Life series. Even at full price, it's worth every penny.

EDIT 9/15/21: After beating the Xen section of the game, I would still recommend the game. The opening level of Xen is breathtaking, packed full of unique environments, incorporates new enemies that still feel true to the game's design, and is an overall great time. Sadly, it goes straight downhill from there. Gonarch's Lair is a slog that turns an exciting boss fight into a lengthy game of cat-and-mouse. Interloper is a chore to play that drags on and on. Nihilanth is a decent conclusion, but it is hampered by Interloper's tediousness leading up to that point. 

While this version of Xen is gorgeous and breathtaking to see, the original Half-Life version is ultimately the better experience. It doesn't overstay its welcome nearly as much as Black Mesa's Xen does. Even if it isn't perfect, the pacing in Half-Life's version of Gonarch's Lair and Interloper is so much better than Black Mesa's.

This game is way more than just a graphical remaster. So many aspects of the original half life have been altered slightly while still staying faithful to the original. They've made a nice touch to the weapon balancing, weapons like the crossbow are significantly more useful in Black Mesa than in the original HL. Or at least that's what it seems like to me. There are only a couple of really minor things that I wish they would have kept a little bit more true to the original, but they're so minor that I can't really even remember them.

Soundtrack is pretty decent. Nothing breathtaking but still alright. Adds pretty good depth to the situation you're in.

I like a lot of the details they've added that they really didn't need to add, like the start up when you get the HEV suit for the first time. There are also improved first person animations during "cutscenes" that are more immersive. You can tell a lot of work has gone into this game, and for an indie company to make all this detail and improvement to the original game is impressive.

And then we get to Xen. Jesus, when I got to it in the campaign I thought I was nearly done with the game but, I bet at least a third of the story takes place in Xen. Massive overhaul to the environment and level design, and it looks so damn good. It actually looks like somewhere that the vortigaunts and other aliens could actually live, instead of the lifeless organic mess of the original. Again, the soundtrack compliments the environments really well. Black Mesa is a phenomenal reimagination of the original Half-Life. Black Mesa not only offers massively upgraded visuals, but also improved gameplay, more engaging atmosphere, better environmental design, and entirely new puzzles and areas to explore. Crowbar Collective went above and beyond with their love letter to Half-Life. Nearly everything is improved. 
The atmosphere is something I want to applaud Black Mesa for right off the bat. The graphics are better, the 2 decade time difference will do that. But what's most important is the attention to every tiny detail in the game's maps. You'll find self-portraits in the offices of the scientists, cafeterias with full-on menus, and the Xen portion of the game even allows a short cultural exanimation of the Vortigaunts. And the random scientists, soldiers, and security guards of Black Mesa feel much more like actual people compared to their Half-Life counterparts. There's a scene very early on where an elevator crashes and kills the scientists inside it. In Half-Life, they just have a generic stock scream and crash. But in Black Mesa, that event has a man banging on the elevator door shouting for someone to rescue them and a woman having a panic attack screaming she doesn't want to die. The absolute horror of a Xen alien invasion is beautifully depicted. There are even more scripted event changes like that, but it's for the best if you discover them yourself. 
Gameplay-wise, Crowbar Collective prioritized changing Half-Life 1's map design and numerous puzzles. Xen is easily the clearest cut example of this. What was once a barren empty wasteland is now a bustling alien world with beautiful wildlife and entirely new enemies to shoot. Gonarch's Lair is no longer done in like 5 minutes, On a Rail is no longer a labyrinth of different pathways, Xen chapters have entirely new puzzles that flow incredibly naturally into the game, and some minor vent segments were removed to help the player stay on task. Some of the enemies have been altered a bit. For example, Controllers now actually control Vortigaunts and have massive screams to alert you of their presence. And the marine soldiers now sample their AI from the Combine of Half-Life 2. Furthermore, the two major bosses (the Gonarch and Nihilanth) have become real boss fights. The Gonarch will have you constantly jumping around to dodge its attacks, constantly firing your rocket launcher in the open arena. And the Nihilanth is no longer just avoid the single projectile and shoot, but an intense clusterfuck of lightining, wind, and explosions. Literally, the only part I hated was the area right before the final boss because of how fucking boring sitting on a conveyor belt was.
And then there's all of the little things that serve as icing on the cake. Eli Vance and Dr. Kliener briefly appearing at the start, further connecting the original Half-Life to its sequel. Hell, there's even a Breen easter egg. Achievements to give you a little something extra to do after you beat the game.  The soundtrack fits perfectly for some scenes, Xen music is easily my personal favorite. 
Some minor complaints I had when playing were mostly visual bugs and errors. The Over-Dark bug drastically ruined my experience though, making it near impossible to see in some areas. The flashlight just not doing anything some of the time didn't help either. Also, the aforementioned Gonarch fight's only cue that it's no longer invincible is the arena you enter.  And Interloper overstayed its welcome a bit too long. 
Overall, I loved Black Mesa. As someone who generally disliked the original Half-Life, I think Black Mesa is astounding. This game is a monument to how dedicated some fans can be.  If you've never played Half-Life, this is the perfect way to start.

Black Mesa is an interesting project; not only because it's a ground-up remake of one of the most influential FPS games in history. It was originally planned as a free mod (and indeed an older version is available for free) but Valve suggested turning it into a paid-for product to the dev team. This relatively laid-back approach to their IP produced the best HL1 experience you can play right now. Then again, it also resulted in the existence of Hunt Down The Freeman, so I guess it balanced itself out.

Good stuff
+ Much improved visuals - textures, particles, character models, etc. This is to be expected since the engine was updated from GoldSrc to Source, but is also looks noticeably better than HL2. As a result, the atmosphere is probably the best of all non-VR HL games.
+ The Crowbar Collective improved on Half-life series' biggest strength - world-building and environmental storytelling. *Most* of the chapters have been changed to be less frustrating and more engaging to the player. In particular, On A Rail and Xen (more on this one at the bottom) chapters have been significantly improved. Virtually all maps have loads of new assets and nice little details added, making them far more interesting places that don't feel as artificial as in the original.
+ Gameplay has also seen a lot improvements, some brought over from HL2 (e.g. AI, physics), some brand new (auto crouch jump, ability to roll grenades). This also includes a combat rebalance - player carries much less ammo for the conventional weapons but enemies seem less damage-spongy. As a result combat is more dynamic and tense.

Bad stuff
- Not a lot of accessibility or UI-related options. Couldn't change crosshair colour which was annoying in the desert area.
- Occasional performance dips, with one instance where the game got stuck below 10FPS for some reason; fortunately, reloading a save created ca. 20s earlier resolved the problem.
- Loading times are kinda long-ish, particularly when a map has to be loaded, so when loading from main menu and when transitioning to a new area. This is pretty standard for Source games but still worth noting.

Xen stuff - a lot to discuss here so pulled it into a separate section
> It's no secret that the last few chapters of HL1 taking part in Xen are considered to be weaker than the ones taking place in Black Mesa. The developers were aware of this and as a result massively redesigned the entire Xen section of the game, which has taken them 5 years. Yeah, it was an ambitious plan but then again the challenge was also huge. The earlier levels have had noticeable changes as well, but nothing on this scale. As a result, the quality of Crowbar Collective's remake was bound to depend in large part on how good their take on Xen was.
> It starts off strong; the first chapter, 'Xen', is quite amazing. The visuals and the ambience are stunning. The gameplay is enjoyable, with a stronger focus on exploration rather than combat. Immediately some improvements are noticeable, with removal of fall damage being probably the most welcome one. All in all, very good start.
> Gonarch's Lair has been massively expanded, with the boss battle now being a huge, tense multi-stage experience. It felt just a tiny bit too long, but still pretty good.
> And then, there's Interloper. Ohhh Interloper... Widely considered as the single worst HL1 chapter, it needed the most amount of rework; but considering the strength of the first two chapters I was cautiously optimistic. The very beginning is pretty good with a fun fight in the vortigaunt village. Unfortunately it quickly goes downhill from there. This chapter is still filled to the brim with tedious platforming and puzzle-solving, with each of the puzzles repeated numerous times with minor variations; what little combat is there ranges from boring fights against the same 3 kinds of enemies over and over, to absolutely terrible (looking at you, conveyor belt fight). You'll be basically forced to main the 2 energy weapons as you will have little to no ammo for the rest. Sure, the dumb rotating platforms are gone, but every bad thing left in this chapter is magnified due to its length. Interloper goes on for way too long, much longer than the original. It's an absolutely excruciating gauntlet of platforming in drab environments -> rehashed puzzle -> annoying fight, repeated so many times that by the end I was completely exhausted and numb to most sensations. I cannot understand how this team of talented developers that managed to improve virtually all parts of the original title dropped the ball so hard with Interloper. If I ever replay Black Mesa I'll use cheats to skip this part. Still, it doesn't quite manage to overshadow the rest of the game.
> The final fight against Nihilanth is much more challenging and interesting than the original. Apart from the insta-death lasers, I enjoyed it. Good fight.

Black Mesa is one of the best video game remakes of all time! I've spent countless hours over the past decade, shooting my way through the Black Mesa Research Facility, and Xen. This game has come a long way from being a mod for Half-Life 2, to how it is today.

Black Mesa: a fan game that has grown into an absolute beast of a single player experience. It's so good that you'd think Valve made it, and I'm not even being dramatic, but it might actually be better than Half-Life 2. (Audience gasps). That's how good this mod is. Take the finesse and polish of the Source engine that makes all of Valve's games look and play so well, then apply that to their original masterpiece Half-Life. Crowbar Collective took a simple little project, 'making a REAL Half-Life: Source' and it blossomed into a lifetime-long passion. Well, I suppose it was a passion when they weren't feeling the crunch. 

The Half-Life community were first teased this brilliant idea all the way back in 2005, and even then there would still be a long wait before we first saw a proper release in 2012. That version of the game featured everything except the controversial Xen segment of the game, which happens to include the final boss. It also had no Hazard Course chapter which served as a tutorial, but this won't ever be in the game as the team have deemed it unnecessary. For years, Black Mesa ended on an abrupt cliff-hanger as you, the player, are teleported to the border-world at the end of the Lambda Core chapter. Finally, after an extremely long wait and countless irritating delays, Half-Life's proper Source remake, Black Mesa, was completed at the very end of 2019. The chapters Xen, Gonarch's Lair, Interloper, Nihilanth and Endgame (now known as End Game) were finally added to the mod, and this segment of Black Mesa is nothing short of breath-taking - I don't care what the haters say. 

Amidst constant criticism over their delays and shortcomings across the years, Crowbar Collective kept their heads held high and gave us the greatest remake of Half-Life we could ever hope for. Ignoring the fact I'm a huge Half-Life fanboy, this really is quite simply the greatest video game mod of all time. It is bursting at the seams with detail, the voice-acting is superb, it retains the campy aesthetic of its inspiration, the game-play is Half-Life at its BEST... and the fact that (pretty much) every chapter is a longer and grander experience makes the entire story last for hours. You'll start slow during the introduction, you'll grab a weapon and start killing aliens, you'll begin fighting smarter enemies like the military, the odds will surmount against you more and more, and before you know it you are humanity's greatest hero battling people and monsters, fighting for Earth's survival in another dimension going head-to-head with whatever terrors await. The A.I for the H.E.C.U soldiers is ironically some of the most impressive I've come across in a shooter, and fighting them is leagues more interesting than the Combine from Half-Life 2. 

I cannot name many games where the fun just keeps snowballing and snowballing without ever slowing down, becoming a more amazing experience as you go until the end leaves you wishing for more. Of course, a lot of this can be credited to the original game, but Black Mesa's ability to keep the game-play evolving as you head deeper and deeper into the deadly science facility just makes it undeniably some of the best video game entertainment you can ever hope to witness. 

This was actually my first experience with any kind of Half-Life content, and even way back then when it was still unfinished it was enough to have me hooked for life. If only Crowbar Collective thought to bring us Source remakes of the Half-Life expansions too... but perhaps we shouldn't be greedy. Do remember to install the Hazard Course mod available in the workshop to truly complete the remake experience. 

The modding community for this game is great too, and there are countless ways fans have added to the developers' vision, in both interesting and just flat-out ridiculous ways. That being said I still can't stress how much this feels/plays/sounds like a real triple-A game and yet it's only a fan-made mod. And not just that, but it's received Valve's seal of approval too, and that's why we can buy this great mod on Steam. That's a true accomplishment! 

The cherry on top of this amazing product is the in-game music. At times it's quite reminiscent of the original Half-Life, and yet at others it goes off and does its own thing, with blazing guitar sounds, piano notes, everything. And even then that music is nothing compared to the utterly incredible music that plays in the Xen chapters. I believe the score conductor's wife provided her angelic vocal range to the soundtrack, and it's almost indescribable how awe-inspiring it is when you take your first few steps in Xen and hear that otherworldly music. You'll just have to take those steps for yourself and see what I mean. Crowbar Collective deserve a serious pat on the back for turning Xen (once a tiny chapter with a pitiful platforming puzzle) into a sparse ecosystem filled with maze-like jungles, water-filled caves, and living, breathing environments decorated with beautiful alien flora. It's really quite the upgrade. The other border-world chapters have also been given the same treatment, all containing enjoyable exploration-encouraging puzzles and fierce battles. 

On the downside of things, I'll admit there can sometimes be frame drops, and there's this weird issue with your suit's torch distorting all the shadow effects in the game for some reason. It almost feels backward to criticise this since I love the sheerly enormous length of this game, but I need to be frank when I say Interloper goes on a little too long, as enjoyable as it is. A chapter that size before the final boss feels a little bit excessive, but I will remind you this is a reflection of Crowbar Collective's commitment to delivering a memorable experience here at this point in the game after years and years of waiting. No kidding, the scope of detail in this game from beginning to end is downright inspiring, and it's a wonder Valve never fully employed these talented developers themselves.

The only thing I haven't touched on is the multiplayer component, and while it's still cool to run around and turn people into piles of gibbed meat, it's got about as much soul and innovation as the original Half-Life multiplayer had. So, not much.  

All I can say is, if you're a fan of single player games that take you on a journey you'll never forget, get on down to the Black Mesa central transit hub and take the next tram to Sector C Test Labs & Control Facilities. Don't forget your crowbar!
