Black Mesa is an FPS developed by Crowbar Collective, and the Definitive Edition was released in 2020.
This is the Source Engine Remake of the cult first Half-Life published in 1998.
The least we can say is that the talented developers have masterfully revisited Valve's masterpiece.

The great scenario of the game originally written by Marc Laidlaw remains unchanged.
The player embodies Gordon Freeman, a brilliant scientist recently graduated from M.I.T., 
working at the Black Mesa Research Center in New Mexico.
During an experiment aimed at analyzing a crystal of unknown origin,
an immense catastrophe of unprecedented scale occurred: a resonance cascade.
Dimensional portals open here and there from which unfriendly aliens emerge.
The army was called in to help stop the invasion, 
but seems determined to cover up the whole affair.
You must do everything to try to get out of there, help your colleagues in difficulty, and destroy what is at the origin of this disaster...

Black Mesa lives by Half-Life's motto of "Run, Think, Shoot, Live."
The game retains the charm of yesteryear, oscillating between combat, reflection, and platform making it original.

Unlike the sadly unloved Half-Life Source, Black Mesa is not a simple port of the first Half-Life to the Source Engine.
Although the maps, enemies and plot are similar, the developers have taken some liberties, refreshing the original work.
The very essence of the game is respected, and even embellished in many areas.
The pace of the combat is much more frantic, the shootouts are dynamic to say the least.
Some complex sequences have been simplified, while others have been largely redesigned.
The game has a much more elaborate and spectacular staging than its glorious ancestor, and sometimes offers great moments of bravery.
We are amazed at every moment,
 since the effect of nostalgia is enhanced by all the new things.

Half-Life has never been more beautiful and immersive than in Black Mesa.
The game pushes the limits of the ancient but still very effective Source Engine.
The graphics are sublime, the lighting and reflections magnificent, 
the particle effects striking… 
The weapons become covered in blood when you pulverize an enemy in close combat, 
the game can be very gory, 
almost giving the impression of playing a modern version of Brutal Half-Life.

The game accentuates its connection with the other illustrious Half-Life games, by borrowing various elements from them, including gameplay mechanics.
It's possible to pick up various objects to clear your path, to burn Zombies using flares, to look for a valve to place on its support in order to use it, to reconnect a cable to a socket, to launch a flammable barrel on the tongue of the Barnacles so that it explodes once it reaches their mouth... 
The sprint system and the flashligt are similar to Half-Life 2, except that they no longer drain the battery of the H.E.V. Suit.

The NPCs are much more numerous and detailed than in the past.

First of all, scientists have a plethora of models, including female ones for the first time.
Female scientists should have appeared in Half-Life 1, but only a few leftovers remain in the Half-Life Alpha and Half-Life Source files.
The models of security guards are also much more diverse and better armed.
Indeed, if they are often equipped with their famous pistol, some have revolvers and even shotguns! 
From time to time you can even lead a small squad of "Barneys" and Scientists.
These valuable allies often interact with each other and have new lines of dialogue, in addition to those already well known.

Some recognizable characters and elements now appear in Black Mesa.
Gordon meets the likeable Issac Kleiner and Eli Vance early in the game.
Vortigaunts communicate the same way as in Half-Life 2. Galanga!
Don't forget Dr. Magnusson’s famous "microwave casserole"…

The enemies are essentially the same as in Half-Life, but with models that resemble some of those in Half-Life 2, including their animations.
In addition to the already well-known Xen creatures (including the iconic Headcrabs, the intelligent Vortigaunts, the fierce Bullsquids and many others), Black Mesa introduces :
the Zombie Torso previously seen in Half-Life 2,
the Zombie Security Guards and H.E.C.U. coming straight from Opposing Force and Blue Shift,
two new variants of Houndeyes, the first one is explosive and kamikaze, while the second is a larger and beefier,
and a sort of underwater Barnacle, undoubtedly drawing inspiration from the unfinished Sand Barnacle from Half-Life 2 Beta.

The Military H.E.C.U. and Black Ops are as tough as ever, and can give you a hard time.
They communicate constantly, attack in groups and are not there to make up the numbers.
Female Assassins are extremely agile and flawlessly precise, 
and have the same Long-Fall Boots as the protagonist of Portal 1 and 2, Chell ! 

Additionally, there may be enemies where there were none in the original game.

Black Mesa is much larger than before, and teeming with life and little details that will delight even the biggest fans.

The weapons are exactly the same as in Half-Life, but are not necessarily picked up in the same place.
Some have a few difference differences in their gameplay, such as:
The 357 Magnum has an Iron Sight, similar to Half-Life 1 in multiplayer.
The crossbow has a real scope at the scope, making it more practical and more realistic.
However, all those guns seem much more powerful and impactful, giving a more dynamic combat feeling than in the past.

The last part of the game, taking place in the "Border World" Xen, has been completely remade.
The artistic direction is totally original and splendid, it's a perpetual visual feast.
It almost feels like we're on the planet Pandora from the Avatar, one of James Cameron's masterpieces of the Seventh Art.
This alien universe is adorned with its most beautiful shimmering colors, mixing caves worthy of HL2: Episode Two, lush jungles, and settings similar to the abyss. 
The firmament is covered with clouds of sparkling stars and a multitude of celestial objects.
This ecosystem made up of several biomes is teeming with life and details of the highest quality.
The flora is colorful, accentuating the exoticism of this distant land.
The local fauna is variegated, and while Boids fly peacefully in the skies, other species are much more harmful.
The aliens that we slay throughout the game are there have new variants.
The Vortigaunts are much more surprising beings than we might think at first glance...
Some areas are very industrialized and mechanical, while others are tribal and primitive, like in the Oddworld games.
Xen contains traces of human activities, there are some installations and devices of all kinds.

The original soundtrack by Joel Nielsen is simply masterful. 
It magnificently accentuates the feeling of strangeness and drama of the events suffered by Gordon Freeman with quite calm and mysterious sounds. 
During the fights, the music is very rock or orchestral and emphasizes the epic feeling of this atypical and mythical sci-fi shooter.
On Xen, the music is as unique as it's breathtaking, composed of captivating sounds and exquisite lyrical female vocalizations.

Black Mesa respects the authenticity of Half-Life by providing it with the necessary new features and accessibility.
Newcomers will love the intriguing storyline, the masterfully orchestrated staging, and its anthology sequences.
While veterans of the Half-Life franchise who have completed the first game countless times will appreciate the improved graphics, realistic physics, dynamic combat, subtle references to other episodes, and all the elements brought by this remake. 
The original work from 1998 is in no way stripped of its charm and is brilliantly modernized, with a delicious touch of fan service added.
This is a must-have game.

[H1]Introduction[/H1]
[I]Half-Life[/I] forever changed the way I play and appreciate first-person shooters. While it wasn’t the first FPS to feature a (good) story, I was impressed by how you get to experience the entire narrative from first-person perspective, by its scripted events, and by its deliberate pacing. [I]HL1[/I] was intense, cinematic, suspenseful, complex, and fun. It raised the (crow)bar of excellence very high.

Nowadays, some developers remaster or remake their hit titles for modern gaming systems. Valve did port [I]HL1[/I] to run on the Source Engine in 2004, but the resulting product -- [I]Half-Life: Source[/I] -- was generally considered inadequate. Consequently, a group of dissatisfied fans, branding themselves as Crowbar Collective, decided to volunteer their time to remaster [I]HL1[/I] properly. It was in this way that the [I]Black Mesa[/I] project began.

[H1]Achievement Unlocked: 15 Years in the Making[/H1]
[I]Black Mesa[/I] started out as a fan-made mod of [I]HL1[/I] for [I]Half-Life 2[/I]. Released in 2012 after 7 years of development, it’s still available to download for free at the time of this review. However, the mod only goes up to the end of the “Lambda Core” chapter. The developers spent an additional 8 years converting the mod into a standalone game powered by the Source 2013 engine, adding more details to many of the levels, and re-imagining and completing the Xen levels. The final product of that Herculean effort is [I]Black Mesa: Definitive Edition[/I].

[I]BM: DE[/I] is a notable achievement. The developers essentially remade [I]HL1[/I] so that the story and aesthetics align with those of the sequels. Because of that, the game’s narrative is more cohesive with the [I]Half-Life[/I] lore. This includes formally introducing players to Dr. Kleiner and Dr. Vance at the Black Mesa Research Facility, and showing the Vortigaunts being enslaved on Xen. I believe these changes will not only satisfy many long-time fans, but also ease unfamiliar players into the [I]Half-Life[/I] game series.

[H1][I]Half-Life 1[/I] for Modern Times[/H1]
My memory of [I]HL1[/I] isn’t as exact as those of players who play it on a regular basis, or who have played it recently. What I remember most about [I]HL1[/I] is the general thrill from playing it, and being in awe of a few prominent set pieces (e.g., stepping out of a drain pipe onto the cliff of a mesa as a fighter jet zooms by). What [I]BM: DE[/I] successfully accomplished is letting veteran players experience similar excitement, suspense and tension when playing it, as if they are playing [I]HL1[/I] for the first time.

The original graphics of [I]HL1[/I] haven’t aged well. Even the level designs, which were ahead of the curve back in 1998, are rudimentary by today’s standards. To remake [I]HL1[/I] properly, the developers couldn’t simply insert models with higher polygon counts, slap on new, high-definition textures, and call it a day. The challenge of remaking a game like [I]HL1[/I] is that it needs to feel contemporary, but also deliver the spirit of the original. I was very happy to see that despite the new visual presentation, [I]BM: DE[/I] is similarly paced and subversive as [I]HL1[/I].

The developers interpreted the original material, remixed level designs to make them feel more modern and less rigid, and spruced everything up with advanced lighting and water effects. They did such a good job with the visuals and elaborating on the levels that I was convinced that [I]HL1[/I] had always looked and played this good. It took me watching playthroughs of the original game to snap myself back into realizing how rudimentary [I]HL1[/I] looks in comparison, and how much work the developers had put in into making [I]BM: DE[/I].

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2607538984

Yet, the developers did show restraint on the interpretation and remixing. They couldn’t and didn’t rearrange the layout of Black Mesa Research Facility too radically, and didn’t add new elements that are too disparate from the original concepts. Some levels are likely easier to contemporize (e.g., “On a Rail”, “Surface Tension”), and some harder (e.g., “We’ve Got Hostiles”, “Lambda Core”). What we end up getting in [I]BM: DE[/I] is some unevenness throughout the many levels, which may be an unforeseen consequence of modernizing a classic game while staying faithful to the source material.

[H1]Xen[/H1]
Let’s address the elephant (or Gargantua if you will) in the room: how are those re-imagined Xen levels? For those unfamiliar with [I]HL1[/I], the original Xen levels were not very good to say the least. Even my co-worker who enthusiastically recommended [I]HL1[/I] to me back in the day advised me stop playing upon arriving at Xen. I didn’t listen, and got to experience first-hand how mechanically and tonally different those last levels were. I believe that many people still hold [I]HL1[/I] in high regard only because the first 85 to 90% of the game was so good.

Crowbar Collective did a really great job re-imagining Xen. They expanded the scope of each level visually and structurally. In fact, the new designs bare very little resemblance to what Valve delivered back in 1998. Instead of sticking with the original pukey yellowish-brown shades, the developers assigned each level its own colour scheme. There’s tranquil, mysterious purple in “Xen”, followed by earthy orange and brown in “Gonarch’s Lair”, and finished off with dangerous red and alien green in “Interloper”.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2609848370

Significant changes were also made to the terrain and flora, with “Xen” partly inspired by the forests of Pandora from the movie, [I]Avatar[/I], “Gonarch’s Lair” featuring an elaborate underground labyrinth reminiscent of Shelob’s lair in [I]The Lord of the Rings[/I], and “Interloper” having an industrial look that reminded me of [I]DOOM[/I]. The expanded variety of colours and environment is a much welcome change.

In spite of the creativity and effort, some purists will not like how these newly designed levels greatly deviate from the original. I didn’t mind it, but my biggest complaint about the new levels is that they’re just too long, so much so that I found they overstayed their welcome. Plus, these levels are much more challenging than what the first 70% of [I]BM: DE[/I] presented. Ironically, Xen in this game feels very much like an afterthought as in [I]HL1[/I].

In the end, Xen is Xen. Despite Crowbar Collective’s best efforts, these last few levels just don’t fit well with the first part of [I]BM: DE[/I]. The transition from Black Mesa Research Facility to the alien world is still as jarring as before. Xen feels like it belongs to a different type of game, like ones that star alien-killing space marines, who make their enemies tremble with fear. You can’t fault the developers too much though, because a remake of [I]HL1[/I] just isn’t complete without these divisive levels.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2609847645

[H1]Final Thoughts[/H1]
I love [I]BM: DE[/I], and I will enthusiastically recommend this game to anyone interested in the [I]Half-Life[/I] game series. Coincidentally much like the co-worker who recommended [I]HL1[/I] to me, I love this game up to the end of the “Lambda Core” chapter only, for I’m rather apathetic about the Xen levels. Yet, I recognize that no matter how you slice it, Xen -- in its original or remastered form -- will be divisive among [I]Half-Life[/I] enthusiasts. So who knows, you may actually enjoy them more than I did! No matter what, the creativity and hard work that Crowbar Collective had put in into modernizing [I]HL1[/I], and redesigning Xen from scratch are praiseworthy. And for that, they deserve not only our thanks, but also our financial support.

[h1]The gist of it:[/h1]
Black Mesa is a vision of some people who wanted to show the newer generations of gamers what it was like to play Half-Life for the first time and despite a rough development cycle, I think they succeeded. 

👍 [u]The good parts:[/u]
+Even with a lot of visual changes BM retains what made Half-Life 1 great
+The Source engine is pushed to its limits visually and some of the Xen maps look unreal. 
+Great gunplay.

👎[u]The bad parts:[/u]
-Performance issues in the alien levels.
-The interloper chapter was pretty bad and dragged on way too long.

[h1]Story[/h1]
Black Mesa does not change anything about the original story of Half-Life 1. If you haven't played the first game, the gist is you are a scientist called Gordon Freeman and you are somehow caught in the middle of an experiment that goes wrong and unleashes hordes of inter-dimensional aliens. Things go bad, and you're involuntarily tasked with helping to deal with the threats, alien or otherwise. When I say otherwise, the experiments that were going on were not perfectly okay and the government sent the army to clean things up, including everyone involved in the experiments. 

Half-Life 1 never had cinematic story-telling or deep lore but the way the story was told was through the level design/locations and what was going on around you. It was a simple yet effective way of describing the story to its players and a lot of amazing classic FPS's did that. 

If you never played the first Half-Life then go ahead and do so but if you want a more modern look to what we received back then, then Black Mesa will be the ideal thing. 

Story rating: 8/10

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
While the engine has changed Black Mesa retains the feeling of the classic weapons with all its ups and downs and yes that does include the Hivehand being a pos weapon that no one uses. 

Half-Life 1 and Black Mesa included have very strong gunplay and you will be forced to use all your available arsenal with a few exceptions. Obviously, some weapons are more fun to use than the others such as the revolver being an overall beast but even guns like the Hivehand which I personally hate, could be useful to other players. 

But shooting isn't exactly the only gameplay mechanic in Half-Life and more so in Black Mesa. In order to progress through most levels, you will need to do some platforming or solve some environmental puzzles. Black Mesa emphasizes more on this thanks to its newer engine and the alien levels will require some thinking and platforming skills. 

Sadly nothing's perfect and while 85% of the vision is Half-Life 1, 15% was perhaps a misjudgment or who knows. I'm talking about the Interloper chapter which is one of the latest maps. It seems the devs had something different in mind when making it and it did not turn out so good. It's visually ugly compared to the rest of the alien levels and it's filled with a big amount of boring puzzles and when your life has been sapped away by this, it gets worse as it now puts you in challenging fights against the same enemies over and over.  The classic alien levels were not great either but at least they were over fast. Black Mesa's ones can take up to 3 or more hours. 

I do have to give them credit for making something functional because despite them being tedious, they seem like a lot of hard work was put into the whole design. Was it needed? Were the years spent on just the alien levels worth it? Most likely no but good job on finishing and making something functional out of it.

Gameplay rating: 8/10

[h1]Audio[/h1]
Compared to Half-Life 1, sound design was obviously improved a lot to match modern times. Weapon sounds, atmospheric sounds, etc. are all shockingly good despite the small team. 

Voice acting is kinda eh and its the only thing I actually wanted them to improve over the classic game but it seems like they just left it as it is and have hired a few more voice actors to do some lines which weren't really that great. Was kinda jarring hearing the same voice actor doing the black guy voice and next to him the same voice and not even a tone change or something. 

What also has been improved or expanded is the soundtrack. I don't even remember the old one having music but Black Mesa does come with some really great music that fits incredibly well with the events around you.

Audio rating: 8/10

[h1]Graphics, performance and tech analysis[/h1]
The source engine is old, no doubt about it but even so, I think the visual upgrade from the original game is perfect. It was no easy task maintaining it as the old game was filled with details but I'm glad they managed to pull it off. The alien levels except for the Interloper chapter look incredible and for a moment you won't even know its the source engine. 

Do keep in mind that even when taking the engine to its limits it still suffers a lot especially in the animation department and performance not being optimized with newer hardware. You'll see some performance degrade in the alien levels and even with a 2080 my frames would drop to 50's. The good news is they are still optimizing the game so it'll probably be good to go before it goes out of early access.

Graphics, performance and tech analysis score:  8/10

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
 Black Mesa took forever to get finished. Was the wait worth it? I suppose it was. Want to re-experience Half-Life 1 as I did? No doubt about it, Black Mesa is the way to go. Recommended at any price. 

[h1]Final score: 8/10[/h1]
95% postive rating and for good reason. Super fun game to play, thank you for a modern Half-Life.

One major problem Black Mesa had was Xen, this has been solved somewhat, Xen has been changed entirely, improved. Though sadly also lengthened. Tedium sets in before you get to the end.

Just like the original, guns feel fine but not great, enemies are bullet sponges and boss fights go on forever, though I must say the final boss rework was very impressive.

Ultimately it's still recognizably Half Life, even if I do prefer the original (ignoring Xen). I would definitely recommend checking both out.

I'll compare this to HL1, which happens to be my favorite single-player game ever.

Things better in Black Mesa:
Graphics, detail
Dialogue
Audio

Things better in Half-Life:
Movement (much better)
Difficulty (HL is harder in a good way)

I don't know about you, but I love to move quick and to be able to control what I do. That just isn't possible the same way as in Half-Life. If you aren't a speeddemon and just want to experience the Half-Life again, but with better graphics and detail, which can make the game more immersive. Go for it. Buy this.

A few friends have already asked for my opinion on this gam-MOD, IT'S A MOD. So, I decided to make a review about it instead of talking about it over and over. As usual, I'll talk first about the bad things, however there's not that many:

First and foremost; the controversy. I've waited for a long time to buy it because I was seriously against what the devs did. You see, time ago, this was a Mod. For free. The Devs had not yet finished it, but left it there for people to test it out. When they did that, they promised that Black Mesa would NEVER cost money, as it was a mod they created with passion to revive a game they love. Well that's kind of bullsh#t because soon after the game arrived in Steam Greenlight, and after a few months it was released in Early Access, still unfinished, and FOR 20€. A lot of people did NOT take this lightly, as it was a God-damn lie which they tried to hide from the Internet. In the end, I waited long for a sale, and I got it on the Autumm sale of 2015.

The second bad point of the game, is that after so many years in development, it's still unfinished. From the start to the Lambda complex, you'll get to see an insanely beautifull recreation of Half-Life, to then get hit in the face with a "to be continued", as the Xen chapters have been in development for a ton of time. To this point it's still not there, but that's not the only thing missing, as there's also a lot of maps missing on the multiplayer. Crossfire, for example, has been my most favorite HL map ever. It's a chaotic mess that I love, and it's yet to be added (devs said it's the next map to arrive). The multiplayer is also kind of abandoned as I rarely found servers with people, although I won't blame the devs for that.

That being said, what we have left is a game so good, it almost looks like Valve made it. The engine has been pushed to it's limits, and it clearly shows. Textures, animations, models; they all look insanely beautiful. Infact, I've only found a few bugs so far, one of them with a strange hitbox of a door, and another about an elevator that gave me ammunition for no reason at all everytime I went into it. The only bug that really annoyed me was the Hive-gun not appearing on my first playthrough. It was nowhere to be found where it was on the original HL and original Black Mesa, and I couldn't find it anywhere else. I was never a fan of that gun, but it seems that it got buffed and wanted to give it a try...

Weapons have been balanced and/or remade to keep them from over-shadowing others. They also can appear in different areas than in the original game (remember the guard you can safe from a zombie early on? He now lets you take a revolver instead of a shotgun, which appears much later on, when the military shows up). The game also gives you a fair amount of challenge along the game, just as it gives you a fair amount of health, armor and ammo pick ups. Exploration is important, as there are a lot of said pickup items hidden in hard to reach areas. NPC's are helpful on it's own, and also have more personality and character than in the original HL game. You actually feel like they are someone who also got screwed because of the aliens, people who are trying to survive as hard as you.

If you haven't yet (for some dumb reason) played the original Half-Life, I'm gonna tell you to play this instead. However, seeing as it's still unfinished, and the price they ask might be too high for some, you should seriously wait for a sale. 10€ would be a fair price, further down would be a must-have.

Oh and, nice job putting the damn hat at the beggining of the game. It's the Gnome Achievement from HL2EP2 all over again.

The only negative thing I can really say about this game from a player's perspective is how long it has taken the devs to finish and release the Xen chapter. (For anyone who for some reason does not know, the Xen chapter is the final chapter in HL1 that takes place on/in Xen, the alien creatures' homeworld.)
BUT they seem to be making Xen MUCH larger, like over 5x larger. Hopefully it will be worth the wait.

The only negative thing I can say from a modder's perspective is how odd it was to understand the workshop upload tool (at least when I used it back in January, for all I know they may have improved something, but I don't see much in patch notes). Instead of it being something you locate in Steam itself, it is just a program in a folder where you installed BMS. And you have to edit your addon's decription, visibility, screenshots, etc AFTER you have uploaded the addon itself which is strange. Oh well, I will forgive it because it isn't even considered a full release yet. I just hope they will fix up something better later on.

Other than that, it is a re-creation/re-imagining of Half-Life 1. Pretty self-explanatory. One of the best revolutionary games ever made, re-created. Some gameplay elements have been tweaked to fit more modern standards, of course. At least playing this can [i]help[/i] with my thirst for Half-Life related things. Only HL3 will quench that, however.
This game is what brought me into the whole Half-Life franchise, I now own every HL game and desire the HL3
Regardless of if you're just getting into Half-Life or already own and played every Half-Life game- this is THE best way to experience the events of Half Life 1.

All I have to really say is - it's still Half-Life.

Notice I didn't say it's still JUST Half-Life.  Because as an iconic game of the genre, there is no "just" Half-Life.

Worth it for old fans and new blood alike.

Bought this when it first came out in early access, and I've played through at least 5 times over the years. Great atmosphere, and nice graphics with everything turned up high. I still have about a third of the achievements missed. Some challenging achievements but nothing grindy or time consuming. Several hidden ones, too. 

Voice acting is well done, and on par with the original for the most part. The only thing I prefer in the original is the Announcement System. The only mod I found to restore it, doesn't do a great job but it sort of works. 

Xen levels are fine, and look very nice. They're much easier to navigate and complete in this version. This version also has a few Black Mesa areas made easier than the original as well. 

The biggest downsides to the game relate to the engine itself, as this game really pushes it to the limit. I think its worth full price, or whatever you can get on discount.
After playing this game you clearly see what is the problem with new fps games with no soul. 11/10. Will remember it 4 life.
